svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four metadata types Cloud Asset Inventory holds, the three ways to read it and the quota on each, the 35-day history boundary and the folder gap, and why a scheduled BigQuery export is the only durable record
svg.title: Cloud Asset Inventory: four metadata types, three access modes, and the 35-day edge
svg.text: A window onto the estate, not a record of it
Everything here can be learned in an afternoon when the question arrives. The history you did not keep cannot be.
Four metadata types, not just resources
Resource metadata — the resource’s own description
IAM policy binding to the resource
Organization policy set on an asset
Access Context Manager policy set on an asset
Policies and the estate they apply to, exportable together.
Two roles, and the gap between them
Cloud Asset Viewer — view asset metadata.
Cloud Asset Owner — view it, and work with feeds.
Both need Service Usage Consumer alongside, and
both grant at organization, folder or project.
Owner is not a bigger reader — it can wire up changes.
Three ways in, and they are not interchangeable
Search
For finding something.
Fielded queries over name,
labels, tagKeys, location, state.
400 / min / project
1,500 / min / organization
Not all resources can be searched.
List and export
For proving something.
A full snapshot to BigQuery or
Cloud Storage, asynchronously.
Export 60 / min, 6,000 / day
List 100 / min, per project
An empty search is ambiguous. This is not.
History
For what changed, and when.
Up to 35 days. That is all.
Organization and project only —
folders are not supported, which
is the governance unit.
The 35-day edge does not announce itself
Assets that have not changed in the past 35 days return their latest status. So a history query always returns
something — it is simply the current state wearing the shape of a history result.
A quarterly audit asks about 90 days. An annual review is not close. An incident found late always asks
“when did this start”, and the answer is usually older than five weeks.
The service is a window. The export is the record.
Schedule an export to BigQuery and keep it. Retention becomes your policy, joins to your own data become
possible, and the 20-per-day analysis cap stops applying because the analysis happens in BigQuery.
Every organization that has wanted this has wanted it retroactively. That is the one way it cannot be had.
The pattern across the last five posts:
Organization Policy is not retroactive. Dry run sees only operations that happen while it runs. Asset Inventory
remembers 35 days. Google Cloud governs well from now on, and reconstructs the past hardly at all.
